title: Post-Katrina recovery and tradition in New Orleans
summary: Recovery is uneven, newcomers arriving, and the city doing things as they always were, with Topsy Chapman and Hank Leo.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow

blocks.x: What’s the recovery status in New Orleans? Has the city come back?

Yeah, I think the inner city part has. The French Quarter obviously. The Central Business District. Those areas are back up. I think there are a lot of surrounding areas that are still hard hit. People are still — the Ninth Ward, the lower Ninth Ward, out in the east they still have a lot of houses that seem like they either need to be demolished or cleaned up. Somebody should come in and do something about them. So I don’t really know. I think that now we have a lot of new people coming to the city. And I don’t think that that’s necessarily a bad thing. You know, a lot of people who think that it could be — I mean like natives of the city. One thing that happened as a result of Katrina, obviously, is a lot of people moved and didn’t come back. But now you have a lot of new people coming in from all over. People — I guess maybe older people too. But I think that’s what New Orleans always was and always will be — people from everywhere, you know what I mean? So I don’t know that’s necessarily a bad thing. Some people view it as not such a good thing in that it goes back to what I was saying about New Orleanians being so protective of their thing, their place. And I’ve heard on different occasions a native, “where are all these people coming from? Who are they and where are they coming from?” But I think that just New Orleans itself, that it’s always been part of New Orleans, what she is.

The one time my wife and I went was actually shortly before Katrina. And we had that experience of walking, it was somewhere near Bourbon Street, but we could hear this music, and we followed the sound, and on the street corner were these kids playing. And I remember they were doing “Stand by Me,” but they had the — and it was so great. And I don’t know if I was naïve in feeling I’m witnessing something that’s been going on for many, many years, and isn’t it great that it’s still happening. I mean is that a naïve —

No. I think. No, not at all. And I think that that’s again, like — how do I want to describe it — New Orleans, it’s like you see all these progressive things going on maybe, in the city, and then, I mean I think about this from time to time, but then like I’ll go to gigs, week after week after week, and I’m playing songs, obviously we are reinterpreting them over and over and over again, but playing songs from the 1920’s and the 1930’s, the same songs over and over again. So what I mean by that is that the tradition of doing those things over and over again for years and years and years is very much the way things work there. So you have that part where people continue to do — it’s like being in a time warp or whatever, you know what I mean? It’s like you have that part where things are done the same from Topsy Chapman, who is a great vocalist there you know. She and Hank Leo are good friends too, and I was talking to her one day and I was telling her, “oh Hank’s coming down.” “Oh you mention Hank, if he comes to my house I’ll cook a gumbo for him.” You know. But you know, it’s going to take some time because,

you know, you can’t rush good food. You know what I mean? That’s just like the way people are. So yeah, so people just do things the way their mom did them, their grandmothers did them, their grandmother’s grandmother did them. You know. But that’s part of what makes it great too. And so, but then you have people who think that’s like the craziest thing, to keep doing things the same way you would for a hundred years. People are like why would you do that? But then I guess it goes to what your value systems are.
